ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A charged particle with mass \( m \) and charge \( q \) is launched from point \( P(a,\ 0) \) on the \( x \)-axis with velocity \( v \) at an angle of \( 60^{\circ} \) to the positive \( x \)-direction into a uniform magnetic field in the first quadrant. It exits the first quadrant perpendicular to the \( y \)-axis and enters a uniform electric field in the second quadrant with electric field strength \( E \). The gravitational force on the particle is negligible.

1. What is the magnitude of the magnetic induction in a uniform magnetic field?
2. What is the time of motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field?
3. What is the coordinate of a charged particle when its velocity first becomes zero in an electric field?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, O is the origin, the x-axis points to the right, and the y-axis points upward. Uniformly distributed black dots are drawn in the first quadrant, indicating the magnetic-field region; multiple horizontal leftward arrows are drawn in the second quadrant and labeled E, indicating that the electric-field direction is to the left. The particle is emitted from point P on the x-axis, P is located to the right of O, and in the figure the velocity direction is obliquely upward to the right, making 60° with the positive x direction. After the particle undergoes circular motion in the first quadrant, it enters the second quadrant from the y-axis; when entering, its velocity is perpendicular to the y-axis, that is, horizontally to the left. Then reason: In the magnetic field, the Lorentz force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the trajectory is a circular arc. Let the center of the circle be C and the radius be R. At P(a,0), the particle’s velocity direction makes 60° with the +x-axis, so the radius CP is perpendicular to the velocity direction, and the direction of CP can be taken as the normal direction making 150° with the +x-axis. At the exit point A on the y-axis, the particle’s velocity is horizontal, so the radius CA is vertical, and the center C is on the y-axis. From the intersection of these two normals, C=(0,a/√3) is obtained. Thus R=CP=√[a²+(a/√3)²]=2a/√3, and the exit point A=(0,√3a). In the magnetic field, qvB=mv²/R, so B=mv/(qR)=√3mv/(2qa). The central angle of the circular-arc motion changes from the direction angle -30° of CP to the direction angle 90° of CA, so Δθ=120°=2π/3. In the magnetic field the speed remains unchanged as v, therefore the motion time t=RΔθ/v=(2a/√3)(2π/3)/v=4√3πa/(9v). After entering the second quadrant, the particle’s velocity is horizontally to the left, its magnitude is still v, and the y-coordinate remains √3a. According to the figure and the meaning of the problem, the electric-field force is opposite to the velocity direction, causing the particle to decelerate to zero. By the kinetic energy theorem qE·s=mv²/2, the displacement along the negative x direction before stopping is Δx=-mv²/(2qE). Therefore the coordinates of the position where the velocity is zero for the first time are (-mv²/(2qE), √3a).
